origin.new: Why did you start this — what was the trigger, what problem couldn't you ignore?
origin.relaunch: What about your current brand MUST stay — the things people recognize you by, the things loyal customers would miss?

a.customerPraise: What do your happiest customers say about you — the words THEY use?
a.complaints: What complaints or negative feedback do you get? Be honest — this is as valuable as the praise.
a.oneThing: What's the one thing you wish every customer knew about you?
a.challenge: What's the biggest obstacle in front of you right now?
a.facts: A few quick numbers: how big is the team, how long have you existed, which markets?

whyStarted.new: You already told me how it began. In one sentence: why does that still matter today?
whyStarted.relaunch: Forget the founding story for a second: why do you still exist TODAY — what would your customers lose tomorrow?

b.worldLoses: What would the world lose if you shut down tomorrow? Impact, not revenue.
b.conviction: What belief drives this company — the one you'd defend even when it costs you?
b.tenYears: Ten years from now: what looks different in the world because you existed?
b.legacy: When people talk about you in 20 years, what should they say?
b.positioningCategory: Which category are you playing in?
b.positioningFirstChoice: And within that category: for whom are you the FIRST choice — and against whom?

b2.visibility: Should your product brands visibly belong to the main brand — or stand on their own?
b2.roleOfMaster: Should the main brand lend them trust — or should they be free to reach audiences the main brand can't?
b2.namingPattern: How should they be ALLOWED to be named — "Brand Product", or names of their own?

c.discovery1: Think of a moment when your business was at its best. What was happening?
c.discovery2: Think of a moment when something felt deeply wrong. What happened?
c.discovery3: What behavior would you never tolerate — not even from your best-paying client?
c.final: Which three to five would you defend, even when it costs you?
c.livedExamples: For each value: one REAL example where you already lived it.
c.conflictRule: Where do two of your values collide — and which one wins?
c.teamFilter: If you hired someone tomorrow: which value is the non-negotiable filter?

d.hypothesis: Archetype hypothesis from your current appearance
d.pairs: Which of the two feels more like you?
d.party: If your brand were a person at a party — how would they behave?
d.never: Which trait should your brand NEVER have?
d.admired: Name a brand whose personality you admire — what is it about them?
d.emotion: What should people FEEL when they interact with you?
d.voiceSamples: Which of these sentences sounds most like you?
d.vocabulary: Which words would you NEVER use?

e.warmup1: What pisses you off about your industry?
e.warmup2: What do you wish more people understood about your work?
e.composition: Tone, length and use of the manifesto
e.anchorLine: Which line is the one you would put on a wall?

ep.vocabulary: Words to use, words to avoid
ep.distinctiveAsset: Which line becomes your verbal signature?

f.nameType: Which kind of name fits you?
f.taste: Name three to five brand names you love — any industry — and say why.
f.noGos: Any words, styles or lengths that are off-limits?
f.criteria: Rate the finalists against the eight criteria.

b.purpose: Purpose is the WHY: the reason you exist beyond making money. Vision is the WHERE TO, mission is the HOW — three sentences, three jobs. Patagonia's purpose does not sell jackets; it wants to save the planet.
b.vision: The vision describes the world once you have succeeded — a picture, not a target figure. It may sit ten years out and still has to give direction today.
b.mission: The mission says what you do every day to get there — concrete enough that a new colleague could act on it. Purpose is why, vision is where to, mission is how.
b.positioningCategory: Positioning is the place you claim in someone's head: a category, and the people for whom you are the first choice within it. Without a category people still compare you — just without your say in it.

b2.model: Four models: branded house (one brand carries everything), sub-brands, endorsed brands, house of brands (brands without a visible parent). Each buys a different kind of trust, and each has a price.

c.candidates: Values are rules of behaviour that are allowed to cost money — not poster words. Survey after survey finds that most employees cannot name their own company's values; that is what happens when the words were picked for their sound.
c.final: Three to five is the working range: fewer says nothing, more nobody remembers. Take the ones you would defend in a bad week, not the ones that read well.

d.pairs: The archetype is your brand's character — it steers voice, imagery and effect. You don't pick it off a list: it comes out of comparisons, because a decision between two feelings is more honest than a menu of twelve.
d.primary: Twelve archetypes in four groups; you get a primary and a secondary one. The primary sets the tone, the secondary keeps it from turning into a cliché.
d.gapReveal: Here your self-image meets the picture your current appearance sends out. A gap is not a mistake — it is the most useful thing on this page, and it gets named plainly instead of smoothed over.

e.statements: A manifesto takes a stand: it should attract the right people and put off the wrong ones. The openers are scaffolding — cross out whatever sounds borrowed and keep what you would say out loud.
e.manifesto: A mission explains, a manifesto commits. It is written to be read aloud, so shorter and sharper almost always wins.

f.nameType: There are nine kinds of names — descriptive, invented, metaphorical and so on. Choose the kind first, then brainstorm: a mixed list always collapses into the safest option.
f.taste: The name is the most repeated element of a brand — it has to be sayable, memorable and protectable. What you love about other people's names says more about your taste than any list of adjectives.
f.checks: The more invented a name, the more protectable it is. What you see here are indicators from public registries and from DNS — general information, not legal advice. Talk to a trademark lawyer before you commit.

rebrand.r1: What about your current brand MUST stay — the things people recognize you by, the things loyal customers would miss?
rebrand.r2: What goes — deliberately? And why that?
rebrand.r3: Why now? What happened — growth, new audience, merger, or the moment you got embarrassed by your own website?
rebrand.r4: What do you NOT like about your current appearance?
